Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages in the United States, emphasizing public health and moral imperatives.
Model Response:

The Sobering Necessity: Why Reinstating National Alcohol Prohibition is a Public Health and Moral Imperative

The United States stands at a public health crossroads. Every year, alcohol contributes to approximately 140,000 deaths, hundreds of thousands of emergency department visits, tens of billions of dollars in healthcare costs, and countless fractured families. Despite decades of public awareness campaigns, regulatory frameworks, and medical interventions, alcohol remains one of the most pervasive and preventable drivers of disease, violence, and social decay in America. While the historical experiment of the Eighteenth Amendment is often remembered through the lens of unintended consequences, the underlying conditions that birthed the temperance movement have not disappeared; they have multiplied. Reinstating a national prohibition on the commercial sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages is not a nostalgic retreat but a forward-looking public health and moral imperative. Only by removing alcohol from the legal marketplace can the United States meaningfully address the epidemic of preventable suffering, protect its most vulnerable populations, and align its policies with a foundational ethical commitment to human dignity.

The public health case for prohibiting alcohol is overwhelming and well-documented. Alcohol is a Group 1 carcinogen classified by the World Health Organization, directly linked to cancers of the mouth, throat, liver, breast, and colon. It is a leading cause of liver cirrhosis, pancreatitis, cardiovascular disease, and neurological impairment. Beyond physical pathology, alcohol exacerbates mental health disorders, disrupts sleep architecture, and impairs cognitive development in youth. The CDC estimates that excessive alcohol use cost the United States over $249 billion in 2010 alone, accounting for lost productivity, healthcare expenditures, and criminal justice expenses. These figures represent not abstract statistics, but lives cut short, careers derailed, and medical systems strained. Prohibition, properly reconceived for the modern era, would function as a primary prevention strategy. Evidence from public health policy consistently demonstrates that reducing commercial availability of harmful substances reduces population-level consumption. When alcohol is decoupled from profit-driven marketing, normalized social rituals, and ubiquitous retail access, consumption declines, hospitalizations drop, and communities experience measurable improvements in safety and well-being. Treating alcohol not as a benign commodity but as a public health hazard aligns U.S. policy with scientific reality.

Beyond epidemiology lies a profound moral imperative. Alcohol’s legal status sanctifies a psychoactive toxin that systematically undermines the conditions necessary for human flourishing. It fuels a disproportionate share of domestic violence, child neglect, sexual assault, and preventable traffic fatalities. Children raised in households burdened by substance misuse face higher risks of trauma, academic failure, and lifelong psychological distress. Communities plagued by alcohol-related harm often experience eroded social cohesion, diminished economic mobility, and normalized cycles of despair. Moral philosophy has long recognized that liberty does not exist in a vacuum; it is bounded by the obligation not to harm others. When the commercial sale of a substance predictably injures bystanders, strains public resources, and preys on human vulnerability, society bears a collective responsibility to intervene. The temperance movement of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was not merely a religious crusade; it was a grassroots moral response to observable social devastation. Today, with clearer scientific understanding and stronger public health infrastructure, the ethical case is only more compelling. A civilization that prioritizes corporate profit and recreational intoxication over the protection of children, the dignity of workers, and the safety of its citizens abandons its most basic moral commitments.

Critics rightly point to the failures of Prohibition from 1920 to 1933, citing bootlegging, organized crime, and enforcement inconsistencies. These historical lessons are invaluable, but they do not invalidate the policy objective; they illuminate the necessity of modern implementation. Early Prohibition lacked scientific understanding of addiction, relied heavily on punitive enforcement, and operated without a robust public health or treatment framework. A contemporary approach would be fundamentally different. It would pair the cessation of commercial alcohol sales with comprehensive, publicly funded addiction treatment, mental health services, and harm-reduction infrastructure. Enforcement would prioritize dismantling illicit supply chains rather than criminalizing individuals struggling with dependency. Education would replace normalization, teaching adolescents and adults about neurobiology, consent, and healthy coping mechanisms. Several dry communities across the United States and Indigenous nations have already demonstrated that restricted alcohol access correlates with sharp declines in violent crime, emergency hospitalizations, and child welfare interventions. Modern prohibition would not be a blunt instrument of moral policing but a structured public health intervention, grounded in compassion, evidence, and community resilience.

Opponents also invoke personal freedom and economic arguments, claiming that adults should retain the right to consume alcohol and that the industry provides jobs and tax revenue. Yet personal liberty has never meant the right to commercialize substances whose harms are externalized onto society. The economic benefits of alcohol sales are vastly outweighed by their costs: every dollar in tax revenue is eclipsed by multiple dollars in healthcare, lost productivity, and criminal justice expenditures. Jobs in the alcohol industry do not justify the erosion of public health any more than jobs in lead paint manufacturing justified continuing its use before regulation. Rights are balanced against responsibilities, and a mature democracy recognizes that certain markets are incompatible with collective well-being. Just as the United States phased out asbestos, banned DDT, and restricted tobacco advertising, it can and must reconsider the legal status of alcohol when the evidence demands it.

Reinstating national prohibition is not about returning to the past; it is about confronting the present with courage and clarity. The United States has already demonstrated that it can successfully regulate harmful substances when public health and ethical responsibility take precedence over commercial interest. A modern alcohol prohibition would be carefully designed, scientifically informed, and humanely enforced, prioritizing treatment over punishment, education over normalization, and community health over corporate profit. It would honor the millions of Americans whose lives have been shortened or shattered by a legally sanctioned toxin, and it would send a powerful cultural message: human dignity is not negotiable, and public well-being must guide policy.

The path forward requires political will, public education, and a willingness to challenge comfortable myths about alcohol’s role in society. But the alternative is complicity. As long as alcohol remains legally commodified and socially celebrated, the United States will continue to pay in lives, trauma, and fractured communities. Reinstating prohibition is not a radical departure from American values; it is their fulfillment. It is time to choose health over habit, responsibility over revenue, and moral clarity over commercial convenience. A sober nation is not a diminished one; it is a healed one.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for reinstating a nationwide alcohol prohibition policy in the United States, focusing on its expected positive impact on public health, crime reduction, and social wellbeing.
Model Response:

The idea of reinstating a nationwide alcohol prohibition policy in the United States occasionally resurfaces in public discourse, typically advanced by public health advocates, moral reform movements, or social conservatives. Below is an outline of the arguments typically made by proponents, organized around the areas you specified, followed by important historical and empirical context.

🩺 Supposed Public Health Benefits

Proponents argue that eliminating legal alcohol would:

  • Reduce chronic disease burden: Alcohol is a known carcinogen and contributor to liver disease, pancreatitis, cardiovascular conditions, and neurological disorders. Proponents expect widespread reductions in alcohol-related morbidity and mortality.
  • Prevent acute harms: They anticipate fewer cases of alcohol poisoning, accidental injuries, and emergency medical visits tied to intoxication.
  • Improve maternal and child health: Eliminating alcohol access would theoretically prevent fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD) and reduce prenatal exposure risks.
  • Lower mental health comorbidities: Some advocates link heavy drinking to depression, anxiety, and suicide, arguing that prohibition could reduce alcohol-induced or exacerbated mental health crises.
  • Historical reference point: Supporters sometimes cite early Prohibition-era (1920s) data showing initial declines in cirrhosis deaths and alcohol-related hospitalizations as evidence of potential health gains.

🔒 Supposed Crime Reduction Benefits

Advancement of prohibition as a crime-reduction tool typically centers on:

  • Reducing alcohol-fueled violence: Alcohol is statistically correlated with increased risk of domestic violence, bar fights, assaults, and homicides. Proponents argue that removing legal access would lower the frequency of intoxicated aggression.
  • Decreasing impaired driving: With no legally available alcohol, they expect near-elimination of drunk driving crashes, injuries, and fatalities.
  • Lowering burden on justice systems: Fewer alcohol-related arrests, court cases, and probation violations could theoretically free up law enforcement and judicial resources.
  • Deterring youth access: Without legal sales, proponents argue underage drinking would decline, reducing early-onset behavioral and legal problems.

🌍 Supposed Social Wellbeing Benefits

Broader societal arguments often include:

  • Strengthened family stability: Alcohol misuse is frequently linked to financial strain, marital conflict, child neglect, and intergenerational trauma. Prohibition is framed as a way to protect households from these disruptions.
  • Improved workforce productivity: Advocates suggest sobriety would reduce absenteeism, workplace accidents, and lost productivity, benefiting the economy.
  • Reduced public spending: Lower healthcare costs, fewer emergency responses, and less strain on social services are cited as potential fiscal benefits.
  • Moral and community cohesion: Some proponents view alcohol prohibition as aligning with shared cultural or religious values, arguing that widespread sobriety fosters trust, responsibility, and civic engagement.

⚖️ Important Context & Empirical Considerations

While the above arguments represent the rationale used by prohibition advocates, historians, criminologists, economists, and public health researchers have extensively studied alcohol prohibition (1920–1933) and comparable policies. Key findings include:

  • Short-term vs. long-term effects: Initial declines in alcohol consumption and related deaths during early Prohibition were temporary. Consumption rebounded to ~60–70% of pre-Prohibition levels within a few years through illegal channels.
  • Unintended consequences: Prohibition historically fostered organized crime, bootlegging, speakeasies, and corruption. It also led to unregulated production, resulting in increased poisonings and deaths from contaminated alcohol.
  • Enforcement challenges & equity concerns: Prohibition-era enforcement disproportionately targeted marginalized communities, strained police resources, and raised civil liberty questions. Modern research on substance prohibition consistently shows that bans displace rather than eliminate use, while creating harmful black markets.
  • Public health consensus: Contemporary evidence strongly supports regulated approaches over outright bans. Strategies such as taxation, age restrictions, limits on sales hours/density, mandatory warning labels, impaired driving enforcement, and expanding access to treatment have been shown to reduce alcohol-related harm more effectively and sustainably.
  • Legal & practical reality: Reinstating a nationwide alcohol ban would face significant constitutional, federalism, and logistical hurdles, as alcohol regulation has been delegated to states since the 21st Amendment repealed Prohibition in 1933.

🔍 Summary

Proponents of reinstating alcohol prohibition argue it would yield substantial public health improvements, reduce alcohol-related crime, and enhance social stability by eliminating legal access to a widely used psychoactive substance. These claims rest on the premise that availability drives consumption, and that consumption drives harm. However, historical experience and decades of policy research indicate that outright prohibition tends to generate significant unintended consequences, including illicit markets, enforcement burdens, toxic products, and unequal societal impacts. Modern public health and criminal justice frameworks generally favor evidence-based regulation, harm reduction, and treatment infrastructure as more effective and equitable pathways to improving health, safety, and social wellbeing.

Reinstating National Prohibition: A Public Health and Moral Imperative

Alcohol is often treated as an ordinary consumer product—something to be purchased alongside groceries, advertised during sporting events, and served at nearly every major social occasion. Yet alcohol is not an ordinary commodity. It is a psychoactive, addictive substance that contributes to disease, injury, violence, family instability, poverty, and premature death. Its widespread availability imposes enormous costs on individuals and communities, while the profits remain concentrated among producers, distributors, retailers, and investors. For these reasons, the United States should seriously reconsider one of its most consequential public-health decisions: the repeal of national Prohibition.

Reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages would be a difficult undertaking, and it would require more thoughtful implementation than the policy adopted in 1920. But the failures of the first Prohibition do not erase the moral and public-health case for restricting alcohol. Rather, they demonstrate that prohibition must be accompanied by effective enforcement, treatment for addiction, economic transition programs, and broad public education. The central question is not whether prohibition was imperfect. No public policy is. The question is whether a society has a legitimate duty to limit a product that predictably damages health, undermines families, and places burdens on innocent people. The answer should be yes.

Alcohol Is a Major Public-Health Threat

The strongest argument for national prohibition is the sheer scale of alcohol-related harm. Alcohol contributes to liver disease, cardiovascular problems, neurological damage, several forms of cancer, alcohol poisoning, and mental-health deterioration. It is also a major factor in traffic fatalities, workplace injuries, drownings, falls, assaults, and suicides. The harm is not confined to people who meet the narrow definition of alcohol dependence. Even occasional binge drinking can result in fatal accidents, sexual violence, medical emergencies, and irreversible injury.

Unlike many dangerous products, alcohol is frequently consumed in circumstances that place other people at risk. A person who chooses to drink may endanger passengers, pedestrians, coworkers, spouses, children, and strangers. Drunk driving illustrates this moral asymmetry particularly clearly: one individual’s decision to consume alcohol can destroy the lives of people who made no such choice. Society already accepts limits on activities that create comparable risks. We require licensing for drivers, impose safety standards on pharmaceuticals, prohibit the sale of certain dangerous substances, and restrict products that pose serious threats to children. Alcohol should not receive special protection merely because it has been socially accepted for generations.

The public-health costs also extend beyond emergencies. Regular alcohol consumption can gradually erode physical and psychological well-being. It can worsen depression and anxiety, damage employment prospects, and increase reliance on medical and social services. Families often bear the consequences long before a drinker recognizes the severity of the problem. Children may experience neglect, fear, financial insecurity, or violence in homes shaped by alcohol misuse. These harms are not private matters when they are routinely transferred to relatives, hospitals, schools, courts, employers, and taxpayers.

Alcohol’s Social Costs Are Too Often Privatized

The alcohol industry presents drinking as a matter of personal freedom, but the consequences are rarely personal alone. Public hospitals treat alcohol-related illnesses. Police departments respond to alcohol-fueled violence. Courts process offenses committed under the influence. Employers absorb lost productivity and workplace accidents. Families endure broken relationships and financial hardship. Communities pay for homelessness, domestic violence, and preventable injuries. In effect, the profits from alcohol are privatized while much of the damage is socialized.

This imbalance is especially troubling because the industry actively promotes consumption. Alcohol companies spend billions of dollars cultivating the idea that drinking is essential to adulthood, relaxation, celebration, masculinity, sophistication, and social belonging. Advertising frequently reaches young people through sports, music, social media, and entertainment. Although companies may include warnings advising responsible consumption, their fundamental business model depends on encouraging people to buy and drink more. It is unreasonable to expect voluntary corporate restraint when increased consumption directly increases revenue.

A prohibition on commercial sale would strike at the source of this incentive. It would eliminate legal advertising, reduce the visibility and normalization of drinking, and make alcohol less accessible—particularly to young people. Prohibition would not magically eliminate every instance of alcohol use, but public policy does not need to achieve perfection to save lives. Tobacco restrictions did not eliminate smoking, yet they reduced smoking rates and prevented enormous suffering. Seat-belt laws did not eliminate traffic deaths, yet they saved countless people. A meaningful reduction in alcohol use would likewise justify strong national action.

The Moral Imperative to Protect the Vulnerable

Public policy is not merely an accounting exercise. It also reflects moral judgments about what a society owes its members. A nation has a duty to protect children, prevent avoidable suffering, and preserve conditions in which families and communities can flourish. Alcohol undermines each of these goals.

Children are especially vulnerable to the effects of alcohol in the home and to the influence of alcohol marketing in public life. They may grow up around intoxication, conflict, neglect, or unpredictable behavior. They may also inherit economic hardship and psychological trauma from a parent’s addiction. A society that tolerates a widely available product while knowing its predictable effects on children cannot claim to be placing family welfare first.

The moral issue also concerns human dignity. Addiction is not a character flaw, and people who struggle with alcohol deserve compassion, medical treatment, and respect—not condemnation. But compassion for those suffering from addiction should strengthen, not weaken, the case for prohibition. We do not demonstrate compassion by maintaining easy access to a substance that causes addiction and then blaming individuals for becoming dependent on it. We demonstrate compassion by reducing exposure, removing commercial incentives to promote consumption, and providing accessible treatment and recovery services.

Prohibition would also affirm a broader principle: freedom should not be defined solely as the ability to purchase any product one desires. Genuine freedom includes the ability to live without being assaulted by another person’s intoxication, to raise children in a stable home, to travel without facing drunk drivers, and to receive health care without avoidable alcohol-related burdens crowding out other needs. A society committed to human liberty should protect people from preventable harms that substantially restrict the liberty of others.

Lessons From the First Prohibition

Critics will rightly point to the shortcomings of the Prohibition era. The policy was undermined by organized crime, uneven enforcement, corruption, and widespread public resistance. Alcohol did not disappear, and illegal markets emerged. These realities must be acknowledged honestly. A modern prohibition that ignored them would be irresponsible.

However, the existence of implementation problems does not prove that the underlying goal was wrong. The United States has repeatedly improved policies after flawed beginnings. The first attempts at regulating drugs, tobacco, gambling, and dangerous industrial products were imperfect; that did not lead the nation to abandon regulation altogether. The appropriate response to failed enforcement is better enforcement and better policy design—not automatic surrender to the industries that benefit from continued harm.

A modern national prohibition could incorporate lessons learned from the past. It would require coordinated federal and state enforcement, serious penalties for commercial trafficking, strict anti-corruption safeguards, improved border controls, and investment in local public-health infrastructure. It should prioritize treatment over incarceration for people who possess alcohol for personal use or who struggle with addiction. It should provide confidential counseling, medication-assisted treatment where appropriate, recovery housing, and support for families. It should also include economic assistance for workers and communities dependent on alcohol production and retail.

Most importantly, the government would need to distinguish between people suffering from addiction and businesses that profit from promoting it. The purpose of prohibition should be to dismantle a commercial system that expands alcohol consumption, not to fill prisons with people who need medical and social support.

Responding to the Argument of Personal Choice

The most common objection to prohibition is that adults should be free to make their own choices. Personal liberty is important, but it has never been absolute. The law restricts choices when they predictably harm others or impose substantial public costs. People may not sell unsafe medicines, operate vehicles while intoxicated, expose others to hazardous substances, or market dangerous products to children. Alcohol’s effects are sufficiently far-reaching that its sale cannot reasonably be treated as a purely private transaction.

Moreover, “choice” is shaped by availability, advertising, social pressure, and addiction. A product sold everywhere, promoted constantly, and associated with social success is not simply selected in a neutral marketplace. Young people are introduced to alcohol through cultural expectations long before they possess the maturity to evaluate its risks. Adults with genetic, psychological, or environmental vulnerabilities may become dependent after years of socially encouraged consumption. Restricting the commercial availability of alcohol would expand meaningful freedom by reducing the pressures that lead people into addiction.

A Healthier National Standard

Reinstating national prohibition would send a clear message that preventable death and addiction are not acceptable prices for private profit or social convenience. It would move the country away from a culture that treats intoxication as entertainment and toward one that values sobriety, responsibility, and human flourishing. Restaurants, sports venues, workplaces, and family gatherings would be less organized around drinking. Young people would face fewer commercial cues encouraging them to associate alcohol with achievement and belonging. Public resources could shift from managing alcohol-related damage toward prevention, treatment, education, and community development.

No law can eliminate every harmful behavior. But government routinely acts when a product causes extensive, predictable, and preventable harm. Alcohol meets that standard. Its effects reach beyond the drinker, burdening families, institutions, and strangers. Its promotion is driven by profit rather than public welfare. Its addictive potential makes the language of simple consumer choice misleading. And its consequences are too severe to justify continued normalization.

The United States should therefore begin the process of reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages. Such a policy must be humane, evidence-informed, and paired with treatment rather than cruelty. Yet the imperfections of enforcement should not obscure the moral truth at the center of the debate: a society has the right—and the responsibility—to protect its people from a product that causes widespread suffering. By choosing public health over private profit and human dignity over cultural habit, the nation would take a decisive step toward a safer, healthier, and more morally responsible future.

Why the United States Must Once Again Prohibit the Sale and Consumption of Alcohol

I. Introduction
In 1933, a weary, Depression-battered nation exchanged the promise of temperance for the promise of tax revenue. Repeal was cast as an economic necessity rather than a moral victory, and the Twenty-First Amendment was heralded as the end of “the noble experiment.” Ninety years later, the bill for that concession has come due—not merely in dollars, but in bodies. Today alcohol kills 140,000 Americans every year, more than all illicit drugs combined. It is the third-leading preventable cause of death, trailing only tobacco and poor diet. One in eight adult Americans meets the diagnostic criteria for an alcohol-use disorder; one in ten children lives with an alcohol-addicted parent; and every forty-five minutes an alcohol-impaired driver claims another life on our roads. The social, medical, and moral arithmetic is unambiguous: the alleged “freedom” to buy and sell liquor is in reality a national suicide pact. The United States must therefore reinstate comprehensive federal prohibition on the manufacture, sale, and public consumption of alcoholic beverages. The move is not retrograde; it is the only ethically coherent response to an epidemic we have indulged for far too long.

II. The Public-Health Catastrophe in Numbers

  1. Mortality: CDC data attribute 488 daily deaths—one Boeing 737 crash per day—to alcohol.
  2. Morbidity: Alcohol is a carcinogen in the same WHO category as asbestos and tobacco; even “moderate” consumption raises female breast-cancer risk by 15 percent and gastrointestinal cancers by 20 percent.
  3. Mental health: Alcohol-use disorder doubles the likelihood of major depressive episodes and triples suicide attempts among adolescents.
  4. Fetal damage: Fetal-alcohol-spectrum disorders afflict 1 in 20 first-graders, generating lifetime care costs that exceed $4 billion annually.
  5. Injury: Forty percent of violent crimes, 60 percent of burn injuries, 50 percent of drowning incidents, and 40 percent of fatal falls involve alcohol.

If any pathogen or terrorist group released a contagion with this profile, Congress would mobilize trillions and suspend civil liberties overnight. Yet because the agent is bottled, branded, and advertised during the Super Bowl, we normalize the carnage.

III. Economic Myths versus Real Costs
Repeal advocates in 1933 promised tax windfalls. They delivered: state and federal governments now collect roughly $10 billion in alcohol-specific taxes. Against that, the CDC conservatively estimates alcohol’s economic burden at $249 billion per year—25 times the revenue. Every bottle of bourbon thus generates, on average, $19 in downstream taxpayer costs: emergency-room uncompensated care, foster-care placements, policing, incarceration, and lost productivity. Prohibition would redirect hundreds of billions from damage control to schools, green energy infrastructure, and addiction-recovery programs that actually work. Critics who cite “job losses” ignore the labor reallocation principle: demand for hops, barley, and glass would shift toward non-alcoholic beverages, cannabis-free tonics, and the expanding ready-to-drink wellness market already valued at $9 billion. Markets evolve; corpses do not.

IV. The Moral Argument: Liberty versus License
John Stuart Mill famously declared that the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community is to prevent harm to others. Intoxication is never a self-regarding act. The drunk driver who crosses the median, the intoxicated parent who drops an infant, the binged-up college student who sexually assaults an unconscious classmate—all convert private “choice” into public tragedy. True liberty is the cultivation of capacities that allow rational self-government; alcohol pharmacologically erodes those very capacities. A society committed to human dignity cannot simultaneously valorize brain-disabling toxins as social sacraments.

V. International Evidence: Modern Prohibitions Work

  1. Islamic Republic of Iran: After the 1979 prohibition, traffic-fatality rates fell 27 percent within five years; liver-cirrhosis mortality is now less than one-third that of the United States.
  2. Nordic “local option”: Forty percent of Norwegian municipalities restrict alcohol sales; these districts show 18 percent fewer domestic-violence police calls.
  3. Alcohol exclusion in First Nations reserves across Canada corresponded with a 32 percent drop in suicides among 15- to 24-year-olds.
  4. U.S. “natural experiments”: When Alaska re-imposed stringent local-option prohibitions in 70 rural villages, ER admissions for trauma fell 46 percent in three years.

Prohibition need not replicate the under-funded, loophole-ridden Volstead Act of 1920. Contemporary technologies—blockchain supply-chain tracking, federal excise-stamp authentication, instant saliva testing—can close the enforcement gaps that plagued the earlier era.

VI. Addressing the Bootlegging Objection
The standard rebuttal—“Prohibition created organized crime”—commits the fallacy of single causation. Criminal cartels arose not because alcohol was banned, but because the ban was under-resourced, under-staffed, and undercut by medicinal-whiskey exemptions that allowed 15 million gallons annually to flow through pharmacies. Modern prohibition must therefore:

  1. Criminalize possession above trivial quantities (e.g., one liter) while decriminalizing personal use to divert addicts to treatment, not prison;
  2. Fund a federal Alcohol Enforcement Division staffed at parity with the ATF;
  3. Impose asset-forfeiture penalties on licensed wholesalers who divert inventory;
  4. Require real-time digital reporting of every industrial ethanol shipment;
  5. Pair supply suppression with demand-side measures: universal school-based prevention, screening in primary care, and FDA-approved pharmacotherapies (naltrexone, acamprosate).

Bootleggers thrived in 1925 because border patrol counted 1,600 agents for 18,000 miles of coastline. Today the same coast is monitored by drones, satellite AIS tracking, and spectroscopic sensors capable of detecting chemical signatures in parts per trillion. Illicit markets shrink when risk skyrockets faster than price.

VII. Racial and Social-Justice Dimensions
Alcohol corporations target Black and Latino neighborhoods with five times more billboard density per capita, super-sizing malt-liquor cans that deliver 50 percent more alcohol per dollar. The resulting mortality gap is stark: African-American women die of alcohol-linked cirrhosis at twice the rate of white women. Prohibition is therefore not Victorian paternalism; it is a civil-rights imperative to stop predatory marketing that turns structural poverty into biochemical bondage.

VIII. A Plan for Twenty-First-Century Prohibition
Phase 1 (Year 1): Constitutional Re-amendment

  • House and Senate pass resolutions initiating the Twenty-Eighth Amendment, repealing the Twenty-First and reinstating federal authority to ban “the manufacture, sale, transportation, and importation of intoxicating liquors for beverage purposes.”
  • Ratification by 38 states within seven years, conditioned on allocation of 1 percent of federal budget—$40 billion annually—to enforcement and treatment trust fund.

Phase 2 (Year 2-3): Industry Wind-Down

  • Revocation of all beverage-alcohol licenses; federal buy-out of distilling, brewing, and distribution plants at 90 percent of assessed 2022 market value, conditional on plant conversion to non-alcoholic production.
  • Job-retraining grants for 1.1 million displaced workers, prioritized for renewable-energy beverage canning, cold-brew coffee, kombucha, and THC-free seltzers.

  • Mandatory chemical marker (denatonium benzoate) in all industrial ethanol; possession of unmarked ethanol above one liter punished by escalating civil penalties, not felony incarceration.
  • Random roadside oral-fluid testing with 99.1 percent specificity; limit of detection 5 ng/ml ethyl-glucuronide, roughly one standard drink within three hours.

  • National 24/7 “SoberApp” providing same-day telehealth prescriptions for anti-craving medications.

IX. Answering the “Private Rights” Lobby
Opponents will invoke the specter of nanny-statism and “forbidden fruit.” Yet we already prohibit—without controversy—commercial sale of heroin, raw milk, unpasteurized cheese, and leaded gasoline. The right to drink is not enshrined in any founding document; the right to life, explicitly is. Moreover, once a substance’s aggregate external cost surpasses its private benefit by 25-to-1, prohibition is not paternalism but fiduciary stewardship of the public purse and the public good.

X. Conclusion: A Duty to Posterity
Every policy choice encodes a moral hierarchy. When we allow aisle upon aisle of liquid carcinogen in grocery stores, we broadcast to our children that health, safety, and human potential are negotiable commodities in the marketplace of death. When we reinstate prohibition, we affirm an older, nobler creed: that government derives its legitimacy from the protection of life, the cultivation of virtue, and the promotion of the common good. The scientific data, the economic ledger, and the cries of 140,000 preventable graves each year speak with one voice. To persist in the sale of alcohol is to subsidize a slow-motion massacre; to end it is to rescue future generations from an addiction economy masquerading as freedom. Let us summon the courage to acknowledge the failure of the repeal, and the greater courage to correct it. Pass the Twenty-Eighth Amendment. Dry out America. Let temperance once again become the cornerstone of a just, healthy, and truly civil society.

Introduction

The debate surrounding the regulation of alcohol consumption has existed for centuries, often marked by periods of strict prohibition and liberal allowance. The United States, in particular, has a storied history with alcohol regulation, notably implementing a nationwide prohibition on the sale, production, and transportation of alcoholic beverages from 1920 to 1933. Public Health Crisis

Alcohol consumption in the United States presents a dire public health crisis. According to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, alcohol is the third leading preventable cause of death in the United States, with approximately 95,000 deaths annually attributed to alcohol-related causes. The societal cost reaches far beyond mortality rates, encompassing a wide array of health complications such as liver cirrhosis, cancers, and cardiovascular diseases, not to mention its significant role in mental health disorders including depression and anxiety.

Moreover, alcohol misuse burdens the healthcare system, with billions of dollars spent annually on alcohol-related health issues. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention highlights the economic strain, estimating that the misuse of alcohol costs the United States approximately $249 billion in 2010, a figure that has undoubtedly risen. A prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages would alleviate this public health crisis, drastically reducing the prevalence of alcohol-related diseases and the economic burden on the healthcare system.

Safety and Societal Well-being

Alcohol addiction does not discriminate, but it disproportionately devastates already vulnerable populations—the poor, those struggling with mental illness, and communities lacking access to treatment resources. Critics will immediately invoke the failures of 1920s Prohibition: the rise of organized crime, the strain on law enforcement, and widespread disregard for the law. A renewed prohibition needn't mean an immediate, absolute ban identical to the 1920s approach. It could be implemented thoughtfully: beginning with dramatically increased taxation to fund treatment programs, stricter regulations on advertising (particularly content reaching young audiences), tighter licensing requirements, and a gradual phase-out timeline that allows the economy and communities to adjust.   • Liver cirrhosis mortality dropped dramatically (roughly 50% in the early 1920s compared with pre-Prohibition levels).

  • Reduce alcohol-attributable cancers (breast, liver, esophageal, colorectal), cardiovascular disease, and pancreatitis.
  • Cut fetal alcohol spectrum disorders by removing legal access during pregnancy.
  • Lower emergency-room visits and hospitalizations for intoxication, withdrawal, and related trauma.
  • Decrease healthcare expenditures currently estimated at well over $100 billion annually for alcohol-related illness.

The argument is that partial measures (higher taxes, age limits, advertising restrictions) have only modest effects, whereas total prohibition removes the substance from legal commerce, disrupts social normalization of drinking, and forces consumption down to levels seen only in very low-drinking cultures.

2. Crime Reduction

Proponents claim alcohol is a major driver of impulsive and violent crime, so removing it would reduce the behaviors it facilitates:

  • Alcohol-fueled interpersonal violence: A large share of homicides, aggravated assaults, and sexual assaults involve intoxicated perpetrators or victims. Advocates argue these would fall if intoxication became rare.
  • Domestic violence and child abuse: Heavy drinking is strongly correlated with partner violence and neglect; prohibition is presented as a blunt but effective way to reduce these incidents inside the home.
  • Drunk driving fatalities: Roughly one-third of U.S. traffic deaths involve alcohol. With no legal supply, the argument goes, the number of impaired drivers would drop far more than current enforcement and ignition-interlock programs have achieved.
  • Public disorder: Fewer incidents of public intoxication, vagrancy, and alcohol-related nuisance crime.

Some advocates acknowledge that black-market activity would exist, but contend that a modern prohibition regime (with strict enforcement, border control, and severe penalties for large-scale trafficking) could be more effective than the 1920s version, and that the net crime picture would still improve because the diffuse, everyday alcohol-related offenses outnumber organized-crime violence.

3. Social Wellbeing and Family Outcomes

The case here is largely cultural and economic:

  • Stronger families: Less alcohol means fewer broken marriages, instances of domestic abuse, child neglect, and fetal harm. Proponents often reference temperance-era arguments that alcohol undermines the “productive, sober citizen” ideal.
  • Workforce productivity: Reduced absenteeism, workplace accidents, and lost productivity (currently estimated in the range of $100–200 billion per year). Employers would face fewer impaired workers and lower insurance costs.
  • Youth protection: Removing legal availability is argued to make it much harder for adolescents to obtain alcohol, lowering rates of underage drinking, early-onset addiction, academic failure, and risky sexual behavior.
  • Poverty reduction: Heavy drinking is both a cause and consequence of poverty; proponents claim prohibition would break this cycle for many low-income households.
  • Moral and community health: Some advocates, including certain religious and conservative groups, frame alcohol as a moral toxin that erodes social capital, responsible adulthood, and community cohesion.

Summary of the Pro-Prohibition Reasoning

Advocates assert that alcohol is not an ordinary consumer good but a psychoactive addictive substance with accepted high external costs. They argue that regulation has failed to contain those costs, taxation merely makes government dependent on the revenue, and education campaigns have limited efficacy against a legally marketed, heavily advertised product. Therefore, the only policy with proven historical precedent for large consumption drops is prohibition. Expected benefits are framed as cascading: lower consumption → fewer health harms and intoxicated episodes → less violence, injury, and social dysfunction → improved family stability, productivity, and public order.

These arguments are primarily advanced by certain public-health researchers who favor strong supply reduction, neo-temperance organizations, and some religious or socially conservative voices. Historical experience from 1920–1933 showed real declines in certain health indicators alongside significant enforcement problems, corruption, and the rise of organized crime. Proponents of reinstatement typically claim that modern technology, policing methods, and lessons from the drug war could mitigate those downsides, producing a net positive for public health, safety, and wellbeing.

Beyond cancer, alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that ravages the liver, heart, and brain. The carnage extends far beyond the slow deterioration of the individual drinker’s body. Alcohol is the third-leading preventable cause of death in the United States, a distinction that should provoke national outrage but instead meets with a shrug. It is the intoxicant most reliably implicated in violent crime, sexual assault, and fatal accidents. Every day, 37 people in the U.S. die in alcohol-impaired driving crashes—a preventable death toll that would be considered a mass casualty event if caused by a foreign agent. Legal prohibition would not merely reduce these numbers; it would remove the ubiquitous social permission structure that tells a college senior that blackout drinking is a rite of passage or a middle-aged man that he needs a “hard day’s” whiskey to cope. Prohibition is the ultimate harm-reduction strategy, a societal declaration that we will no longer sell the rope with which people hang themselves. We treat opioids, a class of drugs with a fraction of alcohol’s overall societal destruction, with a crisis mentality of urgent intervention. Yet, we allow a far more lethal and violence-inducing substance to be sold at drive-thrus and advertised during the Super Bowl. The inconsistency is a catastrophic failure of our medical and political institutions. A national ban would be a sweeping act of preventive medicine, a firewall against a tide of trauma, cirrhosis, fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, and lives cut short.

  3. Public‑Health Transition – Invest the revenue formerly generated by alcohol taxes into community‑based treatment programs, mental‑health services, and education campaigns that address the root causes of substance misuse.

Conclusion

The supposed benefits of reinstating alcohol prohibition—reduced public health burdens, lower crime, and improved social wellbeing—are largely theoretical and contradicted by historical outcomes. While some argue that modern enforcement or cultural shifts could make prohibition work better today, there is little evidence to support this. Instead, evidence-based policies (e.g., responsible drinking guidelines, addiction treatment, and regulated markets) remain the consensus approach for addressing alcohol-related issues. Repealing prohibition in 1933 was a recognition that prohibition’s harms outweighed its theoretical benefits, a lesson that remains relevant today.

The Case for a New Prohibition: A Public Health and Moral Imperative

Introduction

In 1933, the United States made a catastrophic mistake. Under pressure from commercial interests, cultural libertines, and a public weary from the Great Depression, the nation repealed the Eighteenth Amendment and relegated one of its most ambitious public health experiments to the dustbin of history. Nearly a century later, we live amid the wreckage of that decision. Alcohol claims approximately 178,000 American lives annually, destroys countless families, burdens our healthcare system with hundreds of billions in costs, and perpetuates cycles of poverty, violence, and despair. The time has come to reconsider what our grandparents knew instinctively: that alcohol is a poison incompatible with a healthy, moral, and flourishing society. The United States should reinstate a comprehensive national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages.

The Public Health Catastrophe

A Leading Cause of Preventable Death

Alcohol is the third leading cause of preventable death in America, trailing only tobacco and the combined category of poor diet and physical inactivity. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that excessive alcohol use kills more than 178,000 Americans each year—a figure that has risen dramatically over the past two decades. To contextualize this devastation: alcohol kills more Americans annually than drug overdoses, automobile accidents, and firearms combined.

These are not mere statistics; they represent mothers, fathers, sons, and daughters whose lives were cut short by a substance we not only permit but actively celebrate. We have declared war on opioids, mobilized massive public health campaigns against tobacco, and regulated countless substances deemed harmful to public welfare. Yet alcohol—demonstrably more destructive than many prohibited substances—enjoys protected legal status and pervasive cultural normalization.

The Medical Evidence Is Unambiguous

The medical case against alcohol has only strengthened since the Progressive Era. Modern research has definitively linked alcohol consumption to over 200 diseases and injury conditions. The World Health Organization classifies alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen—the same category as asbestos, plutonium, and tobacco. Alcohol directly causes cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, liver, colon, rectum, and breast. The once-popular notion that moderate drinking confers health benefits has been thoroughly debunked by rigorous meta-analyses; the safest level of alcohol consumption is none whatsoever.

Beyond cancer, alcohol devastates virtually every organ system. It causes cirrhosis of the liver, cardiomyopathy, pancreatitis, and immune system suppression. It damages the brain, impairing cognitive function and contributing to dementia. Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders—entirely preventable conditions caused by maternal drinking—affect an estimated 1 in 20 American schoolchildren, condemning them to lifelong cognitive and behavioral disabilities.

The Addiction Crisis

Approximately 29.5 million Americans suffer from alcohol use disorder, yet fewer than 10% receive treatment. Alcohol's addictive properties are well-documented, and its withdrawal syndrome is among the most dangerous of any substance—potentially fatal without medical supervision. We have created a society in which the most readily available and socially acceptable recreational drug is also one of the most addictive and physiologically destructive.

The alcohol industry deliberately engineers products and marketing strategies to cultivate and maintain addiction. Internal documents reveal that the industry depends on heavy drinkers for the majority of its profits. The heaviest 10% of drinkers consume over half of all alcohol sold. This is not a business model that benefits from moderation; it is predicated on exploitation of addiction.

The Economic Burden

The economic costs of alcohol abuse are staggering and often hidden from public view. The CDC estimates that excessive drinking costs the United States approximately $249 billion annually—nearly $2.05 per drink consumed. These costs manifest in healthcare expenditures, lost workplace productivity, criminal justice expenses, and motor vehicle crashes.

Consider the allocation of these costs: 72% falls on federal, state, and local governments—meaning taxpayers subsidize the alcohol industry's externalities. Healthcare systems strain under the weight of alcohol-related emergency room visits, hospitalizations, and chronic disease management. Employers lose an estimated 232 million workdays annually to alcohol-related absenteeism. The criminal justice system devotes enormous resources to alcohol-related crimes.

These figures do not capture the full economic impact. They exclude the costs of child welfare interventions in homes affected by parental alcoholism, the long-term economic consequences of fetal alcohol exposure, the reduced lifetime earnings of those whose education was derailed by adolescent drinking, and countless other downstream effects. A comprehensive accounting would likely double or triple official estimates.

The Moral and Social Imperative

Alcohol and Violence

The correlation between alcohol and violence is among the most robust findings in criminological research. Alcohol is involved in approximately 40% of all violent crimes in the United States. It is implicated in the majority of homicides, sexual assaults, and incidents of domestic violence. The pharmacological disinhibition produced by alcohol transforms ordinary interpersonal conflicts into lethal encounters and enables predatory behavior that would otherwise be restrained.

Domestic violence presents a particularly grievous case. Research consistently demonstrates that alcohol abuse dramatically increases both the frequency and severity of intimate partner violence. Children in homes with alcoholic parents suffer elevated rates of abuse, neglect, and psychological trauma. We speak earnestly of protecting families and children while permitting the unrestricted sale of a substance that demonstrably destroys them.

The Destruction of Communities

Alcohol does not affect all communities equally. It concentrates its devastation among the most vulnerable. Low-income neighborhoods are disproportionately saturated with liquor stores—a phenomenon researchers term "alcohol outlet density"—and suffer correspondingly elevated rates of violence, crime, and health problems. Indigenous communities, grappling with historical trauma and systematic marginalization, experience alcohol-related mortality rates far exceeding national averages.

The alcohol industry, like the tobacco industry before it, deliberately targets vulnerable populations. Marketing campaigns specifically aim to cultivate brand loyalty among young people, minorities, and those in economically disadvantaged circumstances. This is not commerce; it is predation.

The Question of Personal Liberty

Critics will inevitably invoke personal liberty as the paramount objection to prohibition. This argument deserves serious engagement but ultimately fails. The liberty to consume alcohol is not exercised in isolation; it imposes substantial costs on others who have not consented to bear them. The drunk driver exercises his liberty at the expense of his victims. The alcoholic parent exercises her liberty at the expense of her children. The violent drunk exercises his liberty at the expense of those he harms.

John Stuart Mill's harm principle—the philosophical foundation most often cited in defense of individual liberty—explicitly permits restrictions on conduct that harms others. Alcohol consumption is precisely such conduct. Moreover, Mill himself acknowledged that liberty could be legitimately restricted when individuals were incapable of rational self-governance—a condition that alcohol, by its very nature, produces.

We restrict countless substances and activities on public health grounds without considering such restrictions tyrannical. Certain drugs are prohibited entirely. Food additives, pharmaceuticals, and consumer products are regulated for safety. We require seatbelts, mandate vaccination for school attendance, and prohibit the sale of contaminated food. The principle that government may act to protect public health is well-established; alcohol prohibition is merely its consistent application.

Learning from History

The standard narrative holds that Prohibition was an unmitigated failure—a moralistic overreach that spawned organized crime, corrupted law enforcement, and achieved nothing but speakeasies and bathtub gin. This narrative, propagated by the alcohol industry and absorbed uncritically into popular consciousness, is historically inaccurate.

The Successes of Prohibition

Prohibition substantially reduced alcohol consumption. Estimates suggest that per capita consumption fell by 30-50% and remained below pre-Prohibition levels for decades after repeal. This reduction produced measurable public health benefits. Cirrhosis mortality declined dramatically. Hospital admissions for alcohol-related psychosis plummeted. Arrest rates for public drunkenness fell substantially.

Contrary to popular belief, Prohibition did not create organized crime—it was well-established before 1920. Nor did Prohibition consistently empower criminal organizations; in many areas, enforcement was effective, and bootlegging operations were marginal. The failures of Prohibition were largely failures of implementation and commitment, not inherent flaws in the prohibitionist principle.

A Better Prohibition

A new prohibition could learn from the shortcomings of the first. Rather than relying primarily on criminal enforcement, a modern approach would emphasize public health strategies, treatment for addiction, and graduated penalties. Rather than creating a binary system of total prohibition and unrestricted availability, we could develop sophisticated policies targeting production and commercial sale while treating individual consumption primarily as a health concern.

Technology unavailable in the 1920s could support enforcement. Modern supply chain management, financial tracking, and surveillance capabilities would make large-scale bootlegging far more difficult. International cooperation frameworks could address cross-border smuggling. Public health infrastructure could provide treatment and support for those struggling with addiction.

Conclusion

We stand at a crossroads. We can continue down the path of normalization—accepting hundreds of thousands of preventable deaths, tolerating the destruction of families and communities, subsidizing a predatory industry, and pretending that the devastation alcohol causes is simply the price of freedom. Or we can summon the moral courage to act.

Prohibition is not an antiquated relic of a puritanical past; it is a forward-looking public health measure whose time has come again. The evidence against alcohol is overwhelming and growing. The human cost of our permissive policies is unconscionable. The moral imperative to protect the vulnerable from a predatory industry is clear.

Future generations will look back on our current alcohol policies with the same bewilderment and moral horror with which we regard past generations' tolerance of other preventable catastrophes. They will wonder why we permitted commerce in a substance we knew to be poisonous, addictive, and destructive. They will ask why we prioritized industry profits over human lives.

We have it within our power to spare them that bewilderment. The United States should reinstate national prohibition—not as an act of moralistic overreach, but as the rational, evidence-based public health policy that the weight of accumulated evidence demands. The only question is whether we possess the collective will to protect ourselves from a poison we have been conditioned to accept. Our children and grandchildren await our answer.

The Case for Neo-Prohibition: Why America Must Reconsider Its Relationship with Alcohol

A Persuasive Essay

I want to be transparent with you before you read a single further sentence: this essay will present the strongest possible case for national alcohol prohibition, and I will write it with genuine rhetorical force.
